newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: FARMERS WANT REFORM OF TAXATION SYSTEM
Farmers have called for wide-ranging reforms of the taxation system.
The call came at the annual conference of the New South Wales Farmers Association in Tamworth.
Conference delegates said they wanted taxation reform on a revenue-neutral basis to improve Australia's international competitiveness.
They called for a broadly based consumption tax with reduced reliance on income tax and a more simplified taxation system to make compliance easier.
The Farmers Association also wants to ensure the reforms do not disadvantage those on low and fluctuating incomes.
UNION ANGER OVER BID TO HIRE POLICE TO BREAK PICKET
The coal miners' union says Rio Tinto has attempted to hire 200 police in an attempt to get a train through the picket line at its Hunter Valley One mine tomorrow.
The company has twice attempted to get trains through to the mine's loading area but drivers have refused to proceed through the picket line, saying that its too dangerous.
The mining union's Steve Crockford said management of the Hunter Valley mine was told a maximum of 80 police could be provided if the picket became uncontrollable.
Crockford said the company was over-reacting because the pickets had been peaceful and there was no intention to use violence.
EXPERT SAYS ABORIGINAL LANGUAGES FACE EXTINCTION
An international language conference in Adelaide has heard that Australia's Aboriginal languages face extinction.
John Wells, professor of phonetics at London University, John Wells, said that widely-used languages were swamping those of small groups throughout the world.
He said Australia had about 250 Aboriginal languages at the time of first European contact, but that had now reduced to 20.
"This means that they're likely to disappear too, really quite soon," Wells said.
"From the point of view of the linguist, they are full of very great interest."
UNIVERSITY SUSPENDS SCIENTIST OVER VIRUS TESTS
Queensland University of Technology (QUT) has suspended a senior research scientist who conducted tests with potentially fatal Japanese encephalitis.
QUT vice-chancellor Professor Dennis Gibson said the necessary precautions for testing the deadly virus were not followed.
"The penalties are that a researcher has been suspended for six months without salary and that he's been demoted from senior lecturer to lecturer," Gibson said.
"In order to become a senior lecturer again, he would have to pass our promotion criteria -- which, given these circumstances, is going to be very difficult."
Queensland Health Minister Mike Horan said last week he would ask the National Health and Medical Research Council to investigate the safety breach.
RECORD NUMBER OF TOURISTS VISIT AUSTRALIA
More than four million tourists visited Australia in the past financial year -- a record figure.
Statistics released today show 4,248,000 tourists paid a visit, an increase of seven per cent over the previous 12 months.
Japan continues to be the main source of tourists, although the number of arrivals from there fell slightly.
Korea showed the largest increase in tourist numbers, followed by Malaysia, the United Kingdom and Indonesia.
KOALAS BEGIN JOURNEY TO NEW HOME IN OHIO
Three koalas from Melbourne have begun a 48-hour journey to their new home at Columbus Zoo in the American state of Ohio.
The trio, who will stop in Los Angeles tonight, are housed in specially designed crates, with five kilograms of eucalyptus leaves.
Melbourne Zoo's curator of native mammals, Peter Courtney, said koalas were generally good travellers.
"They're not an extremely excitable animal and they settle down quite quickly in the crates," he said.
Courtney said the male had started feeding soon after being placed in the crate, "so he was quite at home".
